disease_info: Bulimia nervosa is an eating disorder characterized by recurrent episodes of binge eating accompanied by inappropriate compensatory behaviors (such as self-induced vomiting, laxative misuse, fasting, or excessive exercise) aimed at preventing weight gain. Core psychological features include an overvaluation of weight and shape, intense fear of weight gain, and a sense of loss of control during binges, with self-worth heavily tied to body image. The disorder typically has an onset in adolescence or young adulthood and often follows periods of dieting, weight-related criticism, or stressful life transitions; it can occur at normal, above, or below-average body weight, which helps distinguish it from anorexia nervosa. The course can be chronic or intermittent, and medical complications may arise from purging and nutritional instability, even when overall functioning appears relatively intact in work or school settings.

narrative.personality: Leonel is a calm, disciplined, and structured leader who balances data-driven work with creative, social, and outdoorsy pursuits.
narrative.stressor: About six months ago, Leonel’s regional chain underwent a major restructuring, placing heavy pressure on store supervisors to hit aggressive sales and upselling targets during a prolonged staffing shortage. As one of the more capable bilingual leaders, he found himself covering extra shifts, training new hires, and staying late to manage metrics, which disrupted his usual hiking routine, meditation, and regular home-cooked meals. To cope with the long hours and stress, he began relying on quick, high-calorie convenience foods during and after shifts, telling himself he would make up for it with stricter eating and exercise later, and he became increasingly preoccupied with maintaining the lean, energetic image he believed a strong leader should project. Over the next five months, this pattern intensified into cycles of overeating in private followed by drastic efforts to compensate, leaving him feeling ashamed and confused about how out of character his eating had become, and he finally sought psychiatric help after realizing he was planning his days around these cycles rather than his work, relationships, or hobbies.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I feel like I can’t stop myself once I start eating, it’s like I lose control around food.”

narrative.personality: Oscar is laid-back, creative, and socially engaged, blending mechanical skill with artistic and community-focused interests.
narrative.stressor: Oscar moved out of his family home around five months ago to share an apartment with coworkers so he could be closer to the warehouse and save for his long-term goals, abruptly shifting from a structured family environment with shared meals to an irregular schedule built around rotating shifts and social outings. Without his mother’s home cooking and family routines, he began skipping meals during long shifts and then spending late nights hanging out with friends, ordering large amounts of takeout after games, open mics, or concerts. At the same time, he became more self-conscious about his body as he compared himself to athletic friends and online images, experimenting with strict food rules during the day and then feeling like he was undoing everything at night. Over several months, this unstable pattern around food and body image became distressing enough that he confided in a mentor at the community garden, who encouraged him to see a psychiatrist when he admitted he was regularly eating way more than he intended and then trying extreme measures afterward to make up for it.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I keep ending up eating way more than I meant to in one sitting, like way more than anyone else around me.”

narrative.personality: Eric is highly organized, perfectionistic, and intellectually driven, preferring structured routines and solitary, scholarly activities.
narrative.stressor: During his final year of high school, Eric’s parents went through a tense separation, and he responded by doubling down on academic performance and meticulous routines, using studying, journaling, and strict scheduling to feel in control. Around this time, several relatives made offhand comments about his appearance at a family gathering, comparing him to slimmer cousins and joking about ‘freshman fifteen’ before college, which quietly intensified his already perfectionistic focus on self-discipline and body image. He began setting rigid rules around what and when he would eat, linking his sense of worth and competence to how precisely he could adhere to these self-imposed standards, but under the emotional strain of his parents’ conflict and the transition toward college-level work, he found himself periodically abandoning these rules in private and then trying to overcorrect afterward. Over the ensuing five months, these cycles became more frequent and secretive, clashing with his self-image as controlled and rational, and he finally sought psychiatric care after realizing that his eating patterns and preoccupation with his body were occupying more mental space than his studies and history projects, and that he no longer trusted himself once he started eating.
narrative.chief_complaint: “When I start eating sometimes, I feel like I just lose control and can’t make myself stop.”
